passage: Clara's water bottle was on the kitchen bench again, the third time that week. At school in Wellington, her spelling sheet had vanished somewhere between her desk and the bus. Yet on Sunday she had spent four straight hours building a cardboard model of a volcano, labels and all. When her dad, Noa, found the bottle, Clara's shoulders went up to her ears. "I know, I know. I'm hopeless." Noa sat down beside her. "You're not hopeless. The volcano took you four hours." Together they drew pictures on a card by the door: bottle, lunchbox, folder, hat. The next morning Clara tapped each picture before she left, and the bottle went with her.

qa.q: What did Clara build on Sunday?
qa.a: She built a cardboard model of a volcano, labels and all.

qa.q: How was Clara feeling when her dad found the bottle, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt bad and ashamed; her shoulders went up to her ears and she called herself hopeless.

qa.q: What choice did Noa make instead of scolding Clara?
qa.a: He reminded her of the four-hour volcano and drew a picture card with her by the door, which worked the very next morning.

qa.q: How does Noa see Clara's forgetting?
qa.a: He sees it as a routine problem, not laziness, because he knows she can focus for hours when something interests her.

grounding: A child forgets and loses things but works for hours when interested, feels bad at reminders, and a picture checklist helps more than scolding.

passage: By Wednesday, Uma's desk in Class 6B held a pile of loose paper, a nest of pencil shavings and no maths worksheet. The class monitor sighed loudly. "Again, Uma?" Uma stared at her knees. In the afternoon, though, when the class began the plant experiment, she was the one who stayed through break measuring seedlings and drawing every leaf. Their teacher, Francis, noticed both. After school Francis taped a small card to her desk with three drawings: a red folder, a pencil, a tick. "Everything with a tick goes in the red folder before the bell. That's all." On Friday the worksheet came back, crumpled but complete. Uma grinned and tapped the card.

qa.q: What did Uma do during break in the plant experiment?
qa.a: She stayed through break measuring seedlings and drawing every leaf.

qa.q: What does Uma staring at her knees suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels embarrassed and bad about being reminded again in front of the class.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make after noticing both sides of Uma?
qa.a: Francis gave her a simple picture card and one rule about the red folder instead of a telling-off, and the worksheet came back.

qa.q: How might the monitor see Uma after watching her in the plant experiment?
qa.a: The monitor might realise she is not lazy, since she worked right through break when something caught her interest.

grounding: A schoolgirl loses worksheets but throws herself into what interests her, and a teacher's simple visual card helps more than scolding.

passage:
Subject: my timetable is ruined
Siddharth bhaiya,
You know my board-exam timetable, the one with green for physics, blue for maths and every half hour planned till March. On Saturday Mausi's flight was delayed, and we all went to fetch her from the airport at midnight. I lost the whole Sunday to sleep. I felt so guilty that I cancelled my cricket for the next two weeks to "pay it back" and stayed up till two redoing the colour codes. Today I could barely read one page. passage:
Afreen asked, "Dhruv, why did you look like a ghost all last week?"
Honestly, Afreen, the planner is the best thing about me. Six colours, every chapter mapped, and I've never missed a deadline. But last Tuesday Nani turned eighty and the house filled with cousins. No studying. I smiled through the cake and felt sick the whole time, like I was stealing hours. That night I set an alarm for four to make up for it, and the next night too. By Thursday I was reading the same paragraph again and again and snapping at my little brother. You know what finally hit me? The planner had no row for Nani. I'd made a plan that could only break, never bend. So now I'm trying something scary: Sundays left blank.

qa.a: Six colours, every chapter mapped.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling during Nani's birthday cake?

qa.q: What turning point does Dhruv reach about the planner?
qa.a: Dhruv notices it had no row for Nani and decides to leave Sundays blank, so the plan can bend instead of break.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's little brother have experienced that week?
qa.a: Being snapped at by a tired older sibling probably hurt, with no way of knowing it came from the four o'clock alarms.

grounding: A teenager proud of a detailed study planner feels guilty after an unplanned family day and answers it with punishing early alarms before seeing the plan must bend.

passage:
Monday. Abhinav pinned his week above the desk: maths and chemistry blocks, one empty evening marked "spare", and lights out at 10:30 every night, written in the same ink as the chapters.
Thursday. The team bus broke down on the way back from the away match, and he got home at nine with the maths block untouched. He looked at the chart, crossed nothing out, and wrote beside it: "Away days need a lighter plan." The maths moved to the spare evening. He was asleep by 10:40.
The following Monday. His classmate Nandini yawned through the unit test after two late nights. "How are you so calm?" she asked. "I missed a day too," Abhinav said. "I just had somewhere to put it."

qa.q: What did Abhinav write beside the chart on Thursday?

qa.a: She may be curious or a little envious, since her late nights left her yawning while his slack kept him calm.

passage:
Nikita, put the highlighter down a minute and listen to your old aunty. When I was sixteen in Aizawl, I had my exam plan in a school notebook, every single day filled. The first time I missed a day, because rain washed out the road to the tuition centre, I cried as if I had failed the exam itself. My grandfather looked at the notebook, and he asked, "Why is there no empty page?" So I began leaving Saturday afternoons blank. When I missed a day, I asked what had got in the way instead of calling myself lazy. And I wrote "sleep" into the plan like a subject. I didn't top the class. But I didn't break, and I passed everything. So, what is your blank page?
Your Lalremsiami aunty

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami miss a day of her plan at sixteen?
qa.a: Rain washed out the road to the tuition centre.

qa.q: What did young Lalremsiami feel the first time she missed a day, and why?
qa.a: She felt as if she had failed the exam itself, because her plan left no room for anything to go wrong.

qa.q: What changed after her grandfather's question?
qa.a: She left Saturday afternoons blank, asked what got in the way instead of calling herself lazy, and wrote sleep in like a subject.

qa.q: How might Nikita take her aunt's closing question?
qa.a: She may feel gently nudged to find room for rest in her own plan, rather than feeling told off.

grounding: An aunt recalls learning as a teenager to leave slack in her plan, treat a missed day as information and count sleep as part of the plan.

passage:
I've shared a room with Suraj for two years, so I know his style. He never books the train until the night before, never picks between two electives until the last hour, and somehow it usually works. When our college fest lost its sound vendor on the morning of the event, Suraj was the one who borrowed speakers from the dance society and rewired the stage in an hour. Nobody else could switch that fast. Our group report was another story. He kept saying, "I'll slot it in when I see the week." On the Friday it was due, his section was blank. I can't say if he was worried; he looked calm. Afterwards, though, he asked me to put a Wednesday reminder on the shared calendar for every deadline. Since then, his part has come in on Wednesdays.
Kunal

qa.q: What did Suraj borrow when the fest lost its sound vendor?
qa.a: He borrowed speakers from the dance society.

qa.q: Why might Suraj have asked for a Wednesday reminder after the blank section?
qa.a: He seems to have realised that his wait-and-see style needs a fixed anchor for shared deadlines, even though he looked calm.

qa.q: What choice did Suraj make after the report went wrong, and how did it help?
qa.a: He asked Kunal for a Wednesday reminder on every deadline, and since then his part has come in on time.

qa.q: What is it like for Kunal and the group when Suraj's section is blank on the due date?
qa.a: They are left let down and scrambling on shared work, even though they rely on his quick thinking when plans collapse.

passage:
Sunday. Chaitanya sent the trek plan to the group: homestay deposits due by Wednesday. Zubin replied with a thumbs-up and "Let's see how the week goes."
Wednesday. The deposit link closed at midnight. Zubin had spent the evening helping his cousin move flats on a whim, and forgot. Chaitanya paid his share, jaw tight.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's tight jaw on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Chaitanya felt annoyed and strained at having to cover Zubin's forgotten deposit.

subtype: Living with a very careful partner or roommate [Receiver]
passage:
Subject: the kitchen, and a thank-you
Hi Yusuf,
First, thank you. Since you moved in, the electricity bill has never been late, and I've stopped waking at night wondering whether the rent was paid. That matters to me more than I've said.
But I want to be honest before it turns into sulking. When you re-stack the plates after I've washed them, or fix the way I've hung the towels, I feel watched. Your chore spreadsheet is great, and I'm keeping it. Can we sort out which things are real needs, like bills and the gas knob being off, and which are just how you like them, like towel folding? The needs, I'll follow. The preferences, can we let go of on my days?
Chai on Sunday to talk?
Irawati

passage:
Two labelled boxes in the fridge, that's how it started. You want to know what living with Jasleen is like? Honestly, it's the safest I've ever felt. She tracks the wifi bill, the cook's leave days and the gas cylinder date, all on a sheet by the door. I haven't lost a key in a year. But in March I caught myself leaving the flat on Sundays just so she wouldn't see me cook. She'd wipe the counter right after me and say nothing, and that nothing was loud. So one night I told her, "The gas, the rent, the locks, those are real, and I'll do them your way. How I chop onions is just mine." She went red, then laughed and said she hadn't noticed. Now I cook on Sundays again.
Shreya

qa.a: The wifi bill, the cook's leave days and the gas cylinder date.

qa.a: She was embarrassed at first, going red, but may also feel relieved to learn of the problem while it was still small.

passage:
Thursday night
Today Kamal wasn't at the morning meeting, and by eleven the whole team was lost. Nobody knew the client's new file names; nobody had the vendor's number. Kamal always has these. He's the one who sends the checklist the night before, catches the typo in the invoice, quietly books the meeting room none of us remembered. We just assume it happens. At lunch Priti said he had messaged in, exhausted, taking two days off. I felt a bit sick thinking how long it's been since anyone said thanks, me included. I'm writing down three things I can take over from him on Monday, and I'll say thank you before I forget again.
Yash

passage: At the community centre's Saturday story hour, Gautam sat between his five-year-old twins. Ojas had already told the librarian about his loose tooth, the dog next door and a dream about trains. Ila sat pressed against his arm, silent, turning pages. "Say hi to the other kids, Ila," Gautam whispered. Ila shrank. Ojas tugged his other sleeve. "Papa, listen, listen!" Gautam felt split down the middle. Then he stopped pushing. He let Ojas sit in the front row and stayed at the back with Ila, reading quietly. On the way out, Ila whispered the whole story back to him.

qa.q: How might Ila have felt when told to say hi to the other kids?
qa.a: She shrank, so she likely felt pressured and uncomfortable at being pushed to act like her brother.

passage: You remind me of myself, Lavanya. At nine I was the loudest boy in our Mysuru school. I could make a friend at the bus stop before the bus came. In every cricket game in our lane I was captain, umpire and commentator. But in silent writing hour I felt like ants were under my skin; I'd hum, and the teacher would send me to stand outside. My best friend Raghu was the opposite. One day he told me, very softly, that he didn't want to play at recess. I laughed and pulled him along anyway. He didn't speak to me for a week. That was when I learned to hear the quiet ones, kanna. Your Naveen Thatha still talks too much, but he listens now too.

qa.q: What three roles did Naveen play in the lane cricket games?
qa.a: Captain, umpire and commentator.

qa.q: What did young Naveen feel during silent writing hour?
qa.a: He felt restless, like ants were under his skin, so he hummed.

qa.q: What turning point taught Naveen to listen to quieter friends?
qa.a: After he pulled Raghu into recess despite his soft no, Raghu stayed silent for a week, and Naveen learned to hear the quiet ones.

qa.q: How might Raghu have felt when his soft request was laughed off?
qa.a: He likely felt ignored and hurt, which is why he kept away for a week.

grounding: A grandfather recalls being a talkative boy who led games and hated silent work, and who once missed a quiet friend's cue.

passage: The rain started just as Rashmi's birthday party began, so thirty children were squeezed into one flat instead of the terrace.
